title: Catching the (Venture) Bus | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z's Jen Kha argues that the traditional 5-10% institutional venture allocation is now the real portfolio error, because ~$3.8-5T of equity value (SpaceX at ~$2T, Anthropic at $965B, OpenAI at $852B) was created in private markets that most LPs have zero exposure to, while buyout returns sit near 15-year lows and AI compresses the software multiples that underpin PE and private credit. The kicker is access: only ~2.4% of 2000-2018 vintage VC funds returned 5x, so resizing venture exposure only works if it lands in the handful of funds that touch the power-law winners.

insights.claim: The costly institutional mistake right now is one of commission — keeping venture 'right-sized' at 5-10% of the portfolio as if it were still a cottage industry — rather than the usual VC worry about bad checks written.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Frames an underweight to venture as an active, accountable decision LPs must defend to boards, not a neutral default — expect allocation-committee pressure to raise VC targets.
insights.quote: The irony, however, is that the mistake LPs may be making today is one of commission, driven by a seemingly prudent question: Is my portfolio appropriately balanced across asset classes?
insights.locator: The irony, however, is that

insights.claim: Venture allocations are typically a sub-slice of a private alternatives bucket targeted at 5-10% of a total portfolio, while endowments run 25-40% — and for some endowments that percentage is mostly NAV appreciation rather than active primary dollars deployed.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: An LP showing a high venture percentage may be passively marked up rather than actively investing — a screen for whether an allocator is truly participating in new vintages.
insights.locator: A few hypotheses. To start, venture allocations

insights.claim: Most LPs encountered by a16z's head of global partnerships have near-zero exposure to the three current frontier model companies — SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI — and no exposure to the leading open-source ones either.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Implies large latent demand for any vehicle offering exposure to these names — secondaries, pre-IPO funds, and the IPOs themselves should meet unusually deep bid.
insights.quote: Every week, I come across an LP who has nearly zero exposure to the three current frontier models (SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI).
insights.locator: A “cottage” no more

insights.claim: Venture loss rates are far milder than the asset class's reputation implies: across a16z's funds, losses equate to just 15 cents for every dollar invested.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'venture is a lottery of zeros' objection used to justify small allocations; useful counter-datapoint in allocation debates.
insights.quote: our losses on investments equate to just 15 cents for every dollar invested across the funds we manage
insights.locator: In venture, no one talks about the mistakes of commission

insights.claim: Concentration inside a single venture franchise can be extreme: one position, Databricks, accounts for 20% of a16z's total AUM.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: An LP's 'a16z exposure' is substantially a levered bet on a handful of names — do look-through concentration analysis before assuming diversification.
insights.quote: Our stake in Databricks alone represents 20% of our total AUM.
insights.locator: But a single winner can have an outsized impact

themes.theme: Private markets now hold the mega-cap tail

insights.claim: SpaceX trades at roughly a $2T market cap and is the largest venture-backed IPO ever by a factor of 10x, with the lion's share of its enterprise value created while it was still private.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Public-market entry points to the biggest tech outcomes now capture only the last leg of value creation — an argument for paying up for private access ahead of listing.
insights.quote: at ~$2T market cap today, SpaceX is the largest venture-backed IPO by a factor of 10x
insights.locator: But the day SpaceX went public

insights.claim: Anthropic is valued at $965B with rumors of a near-term IPO at $2T, and OpenAI was most recently valued at $852B — implying roughly $3.8-5T of combined equity value built largely in private markets alongside SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Two more potential $1T+ listings are queued; index and benchmark composition — and LP relative performance — will be reshaped when they price.
insights.quote: right around the corner is Anthropic (valued at $965B, rumored to be going public shortly at $2T) and OpenAI (most recently valued at $852B)
insights.locator: But the day SpaceX went public

insights.claim: About one third of technology companies valued at $150B+ are still privately held, so public equity indices structurally under-represent the tech tail.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: A public-only tech sleeve is a systematically incomplete proxy for the sector's economics; benchmark risk sits in what you cannot buy.
insights.quote: ~1/3rd of technology companies valued $150B+ are privately-held
insights.locator: So, tech is getting bigger, and more central

insights.claim: Eight of the ten most valuable S&P 500 companies are tech companies, and turnover within that top ten is more dynamic than ever before.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Index concentration plus faster top-ten churn means passive equity exposure is increasingly a momentum bet on a rotating handful of tech names.
insights.quote: 8 out of the top 10 most valuable S&P 500 companies are tech companies (and turnover in the top 10 is more dynamic than ever before)
insights.locator: Power Law is now the shape of our economy

insights.claim: The scale of private financings has re-based so far that Google's 2004 IPO — a ~$1.67B offering closing at a $27B market cap, roughly $3B and $48B inflation-adjusted — would not crack the 20 largest completed VC financings since January 2025, and its first-day cap would be a third of those companies' $75B median post-money.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Historical benchmarks for 'large' rounds are obsolete; underwriting and fund-sizing models calibrated to prior cycles will systematically undershoot.
insights.quote: Today, that offering wouldn’t crack the 20 largest completed VC financings recorded by PitchBook since January 2025
insights.locator: In the good ol’ days (2004), Google went public

insights.claim: Private-company scaling has bifurcated sharply: median time between rounds for actively-raising unicorns compressed to one year in Q1 2026 from 1.5 years in 2024, while 51.2% of companies that once cleared unicorn status have not raised in more than two years.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: A stale-unicorn cohort of roughly half the class is a forward supply of down rounds and write-downs, even as winners re-price upward faster — mark dispersion inside legacy books is about to widen.
insights.quote: median time between rounds for actively-raising unicorns compressed to just one year in Q1 2026, down from 1.5 years in 2024, while over half the private companies that once cleared unicorn status (51.2%, per PitchBook) haven’t raised in more than two years
insights.locator: Further down, the companies with real momentum

insights.claim: Private companies are now generating $1B+ in revenue on timelines measured in quarters, making the unicorn milestone routine rather than exceptional.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Revenue-ramp assumptions embedded in growth-stage models and comparables are too slow; watch for AI-native companies compressing the path to scale.
insights.quote: What was once success in venture (a unicorn) is now your average Wednesday and private companies are generating $1B+ in revenue on a timeline measurable in quarters.
insights.locator: Moreover, the biggest companies in the world

insights.claim: Private equity and venture have maintained roughly equivalent exit counts for a long time, but exit value for VC-backed companies just tripled PE's previous high watermark.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: The historical justification for PE capturing the larger share of alternatives allocations is breaking down on realized-value grounds, not just narrative.
insights.quote: Private equity and venture capital have maintained roughly equivalent exit counts for a long time, but exit value for VC-backed companies just tripled PE’s high watermark.
insights.locator: When venture eats the world

insights.claim: The largest majority-PE-owned company ever to go public was Medline in December 2025 at $54B first-day close, versus SpaceX's ~$2.1 trillion debut close — a single venture IPO roughly 39 times the largest PE outcome on record.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: The outcome ceiling in buyout is an order of magnitude below venture's, which caps how much fund-level return PE can generate from any one win.
insights.quote: SpaceX, the first of the new AI generation, private juggernauts stepping onto the public markets, closed its debut at approximately $2.1 trillion—roughly 39 times as much.
insights.locator: The largest, majority-PE-owned company to go public

insights.claim: The largest majority-PE-backed M&A exit by enterprise value was Aligned Data Centers at $40B in July 2026, while the biggest venture-backed M&A exit was Cursor acquired by SpaceX at $60B.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Venture now sets the high-water mark in trade sales too, and a $60B AI-tooling acquisition by SpaceX signals mega-cap tech buyers absorbing AI-native assets at venture-scale prices.
insights.quote: The biggest venture-backed M&A exit? Cursor to SpaceX at $60B.
insights.locator: What about M&A? In July 2026

insights.claim: Buyout performance has deteriorated materially, with average and top-quartile returns near 15-year lows.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Weak buyout returns plus strong venture outcomes give allocators a performance-based, not just thematic, reason to shift alternatives dollars.
insights.quote: we may be seeing this reflected in buyout returns, where average and top quartile returns are near 15-year lows
insights.locator: It turns out, the next wave of disruption

insights.claim: CalPERS cut buyouts from 91% of new private-equity commitments in FY2020-21 to 58% in FY2023-24 while lifting growth equity and venture from 9% to 43%, and its PE program moved from 30th to 1st among the 30 largest US pension PE programs in three years, with growth/venture now its strongest-performing segment.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: A documented, benchmarkable template other pensions can copy — MassPRIM and the North Carolina Treasurer are already following, implying a persistent flow of institutional capital into growth/venture.
insights.quote: Its PE program went from ranked 30th to ranked 1st among the 30 largest US pension PE programs in just three years
insights.locator: Case in point: consider CalPERS

themes.theme: AI as the solvent of software durability

insights.claim: Vista Equity founder Robert Smith's maxim that 'software contracts are better than first-lien debt' is being invalidated, because the next wave of disruption makes recurring revenue less durable than buyout underwriting assumed.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: The core credit assumption behind a decade of software LBOs is now in question — a direct short-thesis lens on legacy SaaS buyout equity and the debt above it.
insights.quote: “Software contracts are better than first-lien debt”
insights.locator: I’m reminded of something Robert Smith

insights.claim: Earlier private-credit loan cohorts to supposedly uncorrelated PE-backed software companies face compounding stress — AI-compressed multiples, slower growth, higher rates and imminent refinancing — with likely write-offs and no power-law upside to offset them.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Specific, dateable stress point: watch refi walls on software LBO loans from earlier vintages; asymmetry is bad because credit has no winners to offset losers.
insights.quote: There likely will be (and likely already have been) write-offs, and likely no power law of outlier upside to make up the difference, either.
insights.locator: But for those earlier cohorts of loans

insights.claim: Private credit's fundamentals have largely held and the asset class is moving up the stack to underwrite the AI infrastructure buildout itself.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Distinguishes new AI-infra credit (healthy, growing) from legacy software LBO credit (impaired) — the split is where the relative-value trade sits within private credit.
insights.quote: the asset class is evolving in real time, moving up the stack to underwrite the AI infrastructure buildout itself
insights.locator: Similarly, private credit was the coupon-like antidote

insights.claim: Because AI is re-writing the leaderboard for enterprise value and private equity is no more mark-to-market than venture, there may be a large volume of unrecognized pain sitting in PE marks.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Implies PE NAVs are lagging indicators of AI disruption — secondaries pricing and eventual realizations are the tell, not reported marks.
insights.quote: now that AI is re-writing the leaderboard for enterprise value, there may be a whole lot of pain in PE
insights.locator: Plus, this phenomenon isn’t unique to venture

insights.claim: Machine intelligence has already delivered exponential improvements in capability, autonomy and cost before robotics has meaningfully arrived, and innovation will likely keep expanding faster than investors or LPs can map in advance.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Argues the opportunity set cannot be pre-mapped, which favors broad early-stage exposure over top-down thematic sector bets — and flags robotics as the next unpriced leg.
insights.quote: We have already seen exponential improvements in capability, autonomy and cost—and this is all before robotics really arrives.
insights.locator: Machine intelligence compounds the trend

themes.theme: Liquidity, marks, and the DPI problem

insights.claim: The strongest legitimate critique of venture is liquidity — captured by an a16z partner's line about being knee deep in TVPI with no DPI — though the author argues illiquidity is not unique to venture.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Distribution timing, not return potential, is the real constraint on LP re-allocation — track DPI, not paper marks, when underwriting managers.
insights.quote: “I’m knee deep in TVPI, but where is DPI?”
insights.locator: Show me the money

insights.claim: Selling secondaries to manufacture liquidity risks adverse selection because venture returns come from a small batch of winners — 'pruning your roses to water your weeds' — and secondary capital remains a rounding error targeting a very small subset of companies.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Don't model secondaries as a general liquidity backstop for a venture book; the bid is narrow and concentrated in exactly the names you should keep.
insights.quote: you might be pruning your roses to water your weeds
insights.locator: For some managers, secondaries may be the only answer

insights.claim: There is no discount available in the secondary market for the assets buyers actually want — the desirable names trade at premiums to last round.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Buying frontier private names via secondaries means paying up; the 'discount to NAV' narrative applies only to assets you don't want.
insights.quote: And there is absolutely no discount for the assets you actually want:
insights.locator: Secondary Market Premiums and Discounts to Last Funding Round

insights.claim: When a16z offered its LPs liquidity structures on older-vintage positions including a Fund I Stripe seed stake and a Fund III first-round Databricks position, not a single LP chose to sell.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Revealed preference: sophisticated LPs treat true compounders as un-sellable, which chokes supply of the best private assets and supports premium secondary pricing.
insights.quote: Not a single LP chose to sell.
insights.locator: a few years ago, we offered our LPs liquidity

insights.claim: Receiving distributions can be a burden for LPs because they must find a comparable compounding asset to reinvest in and pay interim taxes rather than letting the position grow.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Reframes DPI pressure as partly self-defeating — an argument managers will use to justify longer holds and continuation-style structures.
insights.quote: Ironically, receiving money back is sometimes a burden for LPs because then they have to reinvest the capital.
insights.locator: In my experience, most LPs would prefer to hold

insights.claim: Venture marks are deliberately opaque because a mark functions as a signal of confidence that affects founder relationships and founders' relationships with employees and recruits — and almost every venture manager holds the same company at a different valuation.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Cross-manager NAV comparisons for the same asset are not apples-to-apples; only realized cash after exit is a reliable signal.
insights.quote: At the end of the day, the only true mark is cash in the bank account after an exit. DPI speaks for itself.
insights.locator: Returns over marks

insights.claim: Having a legacy venture book is not the same as having exposure to today's winners — 'proximity is not participation' — because many allocators hold decades of positions with managers who have zero incentive to sell or re-value their books.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Audit look-through exposure to current frontier companies rather than headline venture allocation percentage; stale books can mask a zero position in the AI cohort.
insights.quote: Proximity is not participation
insights.locator: Proximity is not participation

insights.claim: The power law operates at the fund level as well as the company level: the fat tail of outcomes sits within a small group of companies held by a small group of funds.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Manager selection, not asset-class allocation, determines whether a venture increase actually earns the returns being pitched.
insights.quote: Once again, the fat-tail of outcomes is happening within a small group of companies held by a small group of funds.
insights.locator: But, in continuing the theme of power law

insights.claim: Manager dispersion is widening: top-quartile 5-year IRR is now double the median for the most recent vintage, and top-decile funds by IRR have never been farther from the top quartile.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: The cost of picking an average manager is rising sharply — allocation increases into median venture managers likely destroy value relative to buyout alternatives.
insights.quote: Top-quartile 5-year IRR is now double the median for the most recent vintage
insights.locator: Top-quartile 5-year IRR is now double the median

insights.claim: Dispersion shows up in realized cash too: top-decile DPI for nearly 10-year-old funds is 2-3x larger than top quartile and 4-10x larger than median.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Rebuts the claim that venture outperformance is only paper marks — but sets an aggressive bar: top-quartile selection is insufficient.
insights.quote: Median just isn’t good enough. Top-quartile ain’t it either.
insights.locator: And it’s not just paper returns–top decile’s got your DPI

insights.claim: Per Accolade Partners data cited by Aram Verdiyan, of roughly 3,000 US venture capital firms only 20 have achieved consistent 3x net returns over the last two decades.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Roughly 0.7% of firms are repeatably elite — access to those specific franchises is the entire trade, and is itself capacity-constrained.
insights.quote: 3,000 venture capital firms in the US, and only 20 have achieved consistent 3X net returns over the last two decades
insights.locator: In a recent podcast, Aram Verdiyan from Accolade Partners

insights.claim: A September 2026 PitchBook screen of 2,143 global VC funds with 2000-2018 vintages and reported DPI found only 17.0% returned at least 2x, 6.7% reached 3x and 2.4% reached 5x — meaning 83% failed to return 2x and nearly 98% fell short of 5x.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Hard base rates for underwriting any venture commitment: the median fund is a poor use of capital, so a bigger allocation without elite access is a losing trade.
insights.quote: only 365—or 17.0%—had returned at least 2x invested capital. Just 143 funds, 6.7%, reached 3x, and only 51, 2.4%, reached 5x.
insights.locator: Furthermore, a September 2026 PitchBook screen

insights.claim: Venture success is self-reinforcing because a fund that lands one behemoth gains follow-on rights, founder referrals and an information edge that make the next win more likely — access compounds the same way outcomes do.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Implies persistence in venture returns is structural rather than luck, which justifies paying premium terms for incumbent access and discounts emerging-manager diversification.
insights.quote: Access compounds the same way outcomes do.
insights.locator: After all, winning begets winning

insights.claim: Standard diversification logic does not apply to venture allocation because the returns are concentrated in a handful of funds — spreading commitments across many managers dilutes into the 83% that fail to return 2x.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Argues for concentrated manager books over broad venture programs — a direct challenge to fund-of-funds and wide-commitment pension approaches.
insights.quote: In the bigger scheme of things, diversification is something we’ve all been taught to be prudent. But this is perhaps one of the few times where that logic doesn’t land.
insights.locator: In the bigger scheme of things, diversification

themes.theme: Why venture's structure fits this regime

insights.claim: Unlike private equity, venture's power law means the majority of a portfolio can go to zero and the fund can still outperform off a small handful of winners — making venture the structurally correct vehicle for an unmappable innovation cycle.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Explains why venture is argued to dominate PE when technological change is fastest: PE must save every company, venture only needs one.
insights.quote: Unlike private equity, the power law in venture absolves all sins.
insights.locator: Fortunately, this is the kind of ambiguity venture is designed

insights.claim: The fatal errors in venture are not losing investments but investing in the right category through the wrong company, or passing entirely on a SpaceX, OpenAI or Stripe — a psychological asymmetry where misses haunt investors far longer than losses.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Explains why top VCs will pay seemingly irrational prices for category leaders — omission risk dominates their decision function, which sustains elevated private valuations.
insights.quote: If you pass on a company and the company succeeds, you never stop hearing about it–you see it constantly in the press, on X, and in your nightmares.
insights.locator: There are other kinds of mistakes that we do consider fatal

insights.claim: Platform shifts are a threat to incumbents' portfolios but the source of opportunity for venture, which is the article's core reason the asset class should gain share of alternatives during the AI transition.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: The trade expressed as a pair: long venture exposure, cautious on legacy software buyout equity and the credit lent against it.
insights.quote: Platform shifts may keep the other guys up at night, but for venture, it’s where the opportunity is.
insights.locator: Platform shifts may keep the other guys up at night

insights.claim: Institutional investors are not missing the argument for venture — many LPs are making it internally to boards and investment committees — so the bottleneck is governance and process rather than conviction.
insights.speaker: Jen Kha
insights.so_what: Suggests the reallocation is a slow, committee-paced flow rather than a sudden shift — a multi-year tailwind to top venture fundraising rather than a one-off.
insights.quote: Institutional money isn’t missing the argument for venture. Many LPs are making this exact argument internally to their boards and investment committees themselves.
insights.locator: Ripping it to studs and starting over again
